idiom_name: hand-written generic Map helper or a per-context method (loops stay the default)
implementation_notes: Go has no Functor to call: the standard library ships no generic Map for slices (the slices and maps packages provide sorting, searching, cloning and iteration helpers instead), methods cannot be defined on a type parameter, and higher-kinded types do not exist - so 'map for any context' cannot be stated, only its per-context instances. The idiomatic realization is an explicit for-range loop, or one small generic function (func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U) written once for the team's slice-shaped containers, while a user-defined optional or result type carries its own method with the empty branch inside. Since Go 1.23 the lazy form is expressible with iter.Seq push iterators: a stage is a function from one iterator to another, slices.Values/maps.Values supply the source, slices.Collect materialises - the closest Go comes to a composable map, still hand-written per container family. Keep the loop unless the same stage recurs across container types.
pitfalls: A generic helper covers one container shape only: slices, maps, channels and user wrappers each need their own function, so the codebase's 'map' is a family of names kept in sync by convention rather than an abstraction.

iter.Seq stages must honour the yield contract (stop when yield returns false), or a consumer that breaks out of the loop panics on the next yield; iter.Pull additionally needs its stop function called or it leaks a coroutine.

Every helper allocates a result slice per call and cannot inline the closure as reliably as a hand-written loop, so a hot path may pay for the abstraction - the Go blog's own assessment of the iterator style is that 'in many cases a loop will be clearer'.
